metadata.title: How Apps Find a Song's Tempo
metadata.ai_disclosure: Narration is an AI voice (Kokoro af_bella, Rohan V.'s persistent choice for the series); script and decisions by Rohan V.
metadata.note: Audio-concept explainer: how tempo (BPM) detection works. EXECUTABLE EVIDENCE: tempo.py builds a detector the classic way (mel-band spectral flux, 8-s windowed autocorrelation, a log-normal preference centred at 120 BPM as librosa's default, Ellis 2007 dynamic-programming beat tracker) and tests it on 40 synthetic Western drum grooves (grooves.py; no recordings), cross-checked against librosa 0.11.0; every picture and number in B01-B06 comes from that run (evidence/run.log, evidence/scene.json). beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Row-Haan and this video is about how apps find a song's tempo: the B-P-M number a DJ app or a music library shows next to a track. Nobody tells the app where the beats are. It has to hear them. And the hard part turns out not to be finding a beat. It's choosing which one.

props.segment: How Apps Find a Song's Tempo
props.command: How does an app work out a song's BPM?
output: find the gap that keeps repeating
choose which repeat is the beat
props.disclosure: Narration: AI voice (Kokoro af_bella), script by Rohan V.

beats.narration_text: Tempo is counted in beats per minute. At a hundred and twenty B-P-M, a beat lands every half second: the place you'd tap your foot. This is four seconds of a rock groove I generated, with its beats marked. The app gets only the sound, never the marks. Here's how it sounds.

props.title: A Beat Every Half Second
props.sparkLine: The app hears the sound, not the marks.

beats.narration_text: Step one: find where new sounds start. The sound is split into forty frequency bands, and at every moment the app asks how much louder each band just got. Add those jumps up, and you get the onset curve. A drum hit makes a spike. A held chord adds almost nothing. This is called spectral flux.

props.title: Step One: Where New Sounds Start

beats.narration_text: Step two: slide the curve against a copy of itself. At most shifts, spikes miss spikes. At some, they land on top of each other, and the match jumps. This is called autocorrelation. Here, it matches at half a second, and even better at one second. Sixty divided by half a second is a hundred and twenty beats per minute. But sixty divided by one second is sixty. Both are real repeats. So which one is the beat?

I built a detector this way and tested it on forty grooves: rock, funk, house, hip hop, slow ballads, drum and bass, waltzes and jazz swing, five tempos each. Picking the strongest repeat, it got the tempo right on thirteen of forty. Most misses were exactly half: it locked onto the kick and snare pattern, which repeats every two beats. So, like the free library librosa, it adds a preference: tempos near a hundred and twenty count for more, roughly where people tend to tap. Now the rock grooves come out right, five of five.

props.title: Step Three: Choose the Beat
props.sparkLine: A preference near 120 picks the beat.

beats.narration_text: But that preference cuts both ways. Every slow ballad came out double: sixty became a hundred and twenty. Every drum and bass groove came out half: a hundred and seventy became eighty-five. And funk's off-beat kicks pulled it to a different repeat altogether. In all: seventeen of forty exactly right, and thirty-three of forty either right or exactly double or half. librosa, run on the same forty, gave the same verdict on thirty-four. The mistake is so common it has a name, the octave error, and the standard tests score it separately.

props.title: Right, Double or Half
props.sparkLine: Off by exactly double or half: an octave error.

beats.narration_text: A single number has a second problem: real drummers drift. This groove starts at a hundred and twenty and ends near a hundred and twenty-three. A beat grid at one fixed tempo is more than fifty milliseconds off within six seconds, and up to a hundred and forty. A beat tracker places each beat on a strong hit while keeping the spacing steady. That's the method librosa uses, from a 2007 research paper. Half its beats land within six milliseconds.

props.title: Real Drummers Drift
props.sparkLine: Follow the hits, not a fixed grid.

beats.narration_text: So when your app shows a tempo that feels wrong, check whether it's exactly half or double what you'd tap. DJ apps let you halve or double the number, or set a B-P-M range so it can't happen. And for a live recording, check the beat grid, not just the number.

props.title: When the BPM Looks Wrong
props.lede: Most wrong tempos are exactly double or half.
steps: Tap along: is the number double or half what you tap?
Halve or double it, or set a BPM range.
On a live recording, check the beat grid, not just the number.
props.sparkLine: Trust your foot, then fix the number.

beats.narration_text: Find the hits, find the repeat, then choose the beat. I'm Row-Haan, for Humanitarians AI.

props.title: How Apps Find a Song's Tempo
